title: Estefania Ajcip's Sculptural Paintings Unite the Memories of a Separated Family
description: Through vivid sculptural paintings, Los Angeles-based artist Estefania Ajcip peers in on the fractures families face when split apart. Ajcip spent
body:
Through vivid sculptural paintings, Los Angeles-based artist Estefania Ajcip peers in on the fractures families face when split apart. Ajcip spent much of her childhood in Guatemala, while her father worked in L.A. and missed pivotal moments of her youth. In a new body of work titled Folded Memories, the artist contends with this adolescent experience, extrapolating her recollections into poignant compositions filled with a longing for connection.
From birch plywood, papier mache, small LED lights, and acrylic, Ajcip constructs a surreal world in which childhood grief and dreams converge. She often works from family photos, pulling scenes and objects from her home and pushing them into a fantastical realm. “Momo 2012,” for example, depicts two adults grasping hands, while an opening in the wood reveals a forlorn girl and her paper train set. 
“Telephone game” (2026), birch plywood sheet, foam board, thread, matte gel, acrylic on panel, 36 x 24 x 8 inches
Separations and fissures recur throughout the pieces, evoking the distance between Acjip and her father, while new details are revealed or concealed depending on the viewer’s perspective. In “Telephone game,” the artist appears with a paper phone and string held up to her ear, while her father stands at a public payphone that juts out from the two-dimensional canvas.
A similar perspective shift occurs in “Four paths/Two paths?” as a sculptural bus shuttling between L.A. and Guatemala. The latter’s national bird flutters at the vehicle’s front window, leading the way as a symbol of togetherness and hope. A statement adds that the piece most directly confronts “the familial unity that Ajcip so longed for throughout her childhood. Across the exhibition, Ajcip makes clear again and again how the longing that defined her youth now fuels her art, a powerful reminder that strength often grows in adversity.”
Folded Memories is on view through August 22 at Charlie James Gallery in Los Angeles. You also might be interested in the architectural portraits of Arghavan Khosravi.

title: Art Problems: How Do I Get the Guggenheim Fellowship?
description:
Community
                Tired of getting rejected year after year? Don't despair. Paddy Johnson is here to help.
body:
Community
                Tired of getting rejected year after year? Don't despair. Paddy Johnson is here to help. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            I've applied for the Guggenheim Fellowship for the last five years and got rejected every time. I believe I meet the required qualifications. Is this even worth doing? Please help! —Beverly, LA Almost everyone gets rejected. Almost everyone applies more than once. Is it worth doing? That answer depends on information I don’t have. Let’s start with your time. The application process takes a lot of it. If you don’t have much time, don’t apply. The Foundation requests two four-page documents outlining your art-making plan for the year and your qualifications; three references; a list of significant work; work samples; and other basic information about yourself. You don’t put all of that together in a couple of hours. Most artists I work with spend at least a month on the application. You probably won’t win the award. I say that with empathy. In 2026, according to their press release, the Guggenheim Fellowship awarded 223 mid-career fellows between $60,000-$70,000 in 55 different fields of study. Of those recipients, 30 were in fine art and 19 in photography.

title: At This Year's Rencontres d'Arles, Photography Rethinks Its Centers
description:
Features
                The art world at times imagines itself outside politics, or at least agrees on them; the latest edition
body:
Features
                The art world at times imagines itself outside politics, or at least agrees on them; the latest edition of the annual festival reveals otherwise.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Thato Toeba, "civilians I "(2025), collage, glass and wood (photo Mario Todeschini, courtesy the artist and Stevenson, Cape Town / Amsterdam; all other photos Daniela Mayer/Hyperallergic unless noted)
    
        
            ARLES, France — When the 57th Rencontres d’Arles photography festival opened in the second week of July, its 47 exhibitions filled the ancient churches, modern galleries, and unconventional venues of Arles with contemporary photographs, and almost no air conditioning. Sweaty yet jovial visitors moved through Roman and medieval structures and along bustling streets lined with Parisian-priced cafés, carrying personal Evian misters and plastic spinning fans, new staples of the European summer in the age of climate crisis. Opening week drew 22,000 people, nearly half the population of Arles, a small French city on the Rhône once home to Vincent Van Gogh, yet everyone appeared to know everyone, or at least to know who everyone was. The festival runs through October 4, with a season pass costing €42 euros.More than 115 public events took place over the first week — artist panels, curator tours, book signings at the Arles Books Fair, an open-air cinema program by the documentary platform Tënk, sponsored parties that ran into the small hours — and the majority were free. Some ancillary, unofficial, art-world gatherings required an invitation; the rest simply required knowing where they were happening. “It doesn’t have as much pretension as a lot of the other [art] events — although people who have been coming longer would probably push back on that,” said Perry Shimon, a contributing editor at Autre and curator of Filoxenia: Queer Joy in the Mediterranean, a film and photographic project showcased at the festival.Charlotte Yonga featured in The Best Possible Way to Tell the Truth… curated by Nadine HounkpatinDirector Christoph Wiesner wrote in the catalog that “as everything pushes toward simplification, division and reduction,” the 57th edition of the Rencontres d'Arles would create a space for “complexity and attentiveness.” This year, that center space is given over to those whom the Western canon long consigned to its margins — though the festival itself avoids this vocabulary.

title: Chris Kraus, Venice Pavilions, Rina Banerjee
description:
Weekly Newsletter

body:
Weekly Newsletter
                Our favorite national pavilions at the Venice Biennale, Shirley Tse and Dana Berman Duff’s breathing moons, and Dean Millien’s aluminum-foil animal world. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            “After New York, Aruba,” instructs a subway ad with a video showing waves softly crashing against the rocks of a tropical island. My immediate response is to Google where Aruba is.Oh, yes, of course. It’s a small Caribbean island just 18 miles north of Venezuela and it’s said to belong to the Kingdom of the Netherlands, home to the original Prince of Orange. We’ve been talking at the office about retiring the term “Golden Age” to describe the bloodiest peaks of Dutch colonialism. One land’s golden age is another’s inferno. The Netherlands shone brightest with gold that was never theirs. Our own King of Orange has another island on his mind. It’s in the Persian Gulf and it sits on a sea of black gold. He thought the Iran war would be a quick in-and-out like Venezuela, but got his fat ass stuck in a narrow strait. He’s still trying to checkmate the Iranians. Someone should tell him that the term comes from the Farsi words Shah Mat, meaning: the king is dead. Back at work, I run an interview that Chris Kraus did with artists Shirley Tse and Dana Berman Duff. They put up a show full of moons, but it’s really about us. People say that Kraus represents the apex of “90s cool.” I once gave her book I Love Dick to a girl in the hope that she’d love me. She read it and concluded that I was a dick. She ended up marrying me anyway. I still have fond memories of Venice in May. Nothing beats starting the day with a couple of espressos and a sweet lemon soda that comes with a slice of actual lemon on top. I was telling someone yesterday how I teared up several times during this biennale when I was face-to-face with the power and beauty of solidarity. I wouldn’t mind going back for another tour of the show. If you ask me, there’s no better time to visit the biennale than the fall.And after Venice, Aruba.—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

	
		
			National Pavilions We Loved at the Venice Biennale
		
	
	
		You’ve followed our on-the-ground reporting from the consequential 2026 Venice Biennale, running through November 22. You’ve read, I hope, our reviews of Koyo Kouoh’s posthumous main exhibition In Minor Keys, Alma Allen’s unmemorable United States pavilion, and Gabrielle Goliath’s Elegy — displayed at a church after being cancelled by the South African pavilion. You’ve engaged with our coverage of Dayanita Singh’s project at the State Archives of Venice; Arthur Jafa and Richard Prince’s hit-and-miss collaboration; an interview with Khaled Sabsabi, whose Australian pavilion was censored under pressure from pro-Israel groups and later reinstated; and much more from the international exhibition and its collateral events.

But we never got to tell you what we really thought of the national pavilions, and which ones you should visit or avoid. As the punishing heat waves of this summer taper off, this might be the perfect time to visit the biennale, if you haven’t already. Below is the first part of a conversation between Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian and critic Aruna D’Souza on which pavilions they liked, disliked, or remain torn about. They begin with a provocative argument in favor of national pavilions. Did they suddenly become nation-state stans? No, hold on, hear them out. — Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

title: Marseille Museum President Accused of Sexual Misconduct, Putting Institution ‘At Risk’: Report
description: A scathing report by French government investigators accuses Pierre-Olivier Costa, the recently suspended president of Marseille’s Musée des civilis
body:
A scathing report by French government investigators accuses Pierre-Olivier Costa, the recently suspended president of Marseille’s Musée des civilisations de l’Europe et de la Méditerranée (MuCEM), of sexual and moral harassment, breaching rules for granting public contracts, and putting the southern French city’s only national museum “at risk,” according to a Le Monde investigation. 

	A front-page scoop published Friday evening in France also reveals that Marseille’s public prosecutor has expanded an ongoing criminal investigation into Costa’s time as president of Marseille’s top museum, notably amid allegations that he unlawfully used preferential treatment to award contracts and hire at the public institution. The museum’s managing director, Véronique Haché, is also named in the report for related, alleged misconduct.  
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The much-anticipated investigation “identifies numerous breaches by the management — the president and the managing director —  of their ethical obligations, including remarks of a sexual, sexist, or degrading nature, inappropriate behavior by the president, intrusions into private life, suspicions of favoritism in hiring and salary policies, and disloyalty to the supervising authority [the Ministry of Culture],” states the report by the government-operated l’inspection générale des affaires culturelles (IGAC) [General Inspectorate of Cultural Affairs]. “Beyond the sense of distress, it is the institution itself that is now at risk,” it added.

	In late June, Costa and Haché were both suspended from their roles for a period of four months, following the IGAC’s then-undisclosed report into allegations of workplace and sexual harassment. That news surprised many who knew Costa was close to France’s first lady, Brigitte Macron, for whom he served as chief of staff before taking the Mucem leadership role in 2022. Costa is also a former advisor to French President Emmanuel Macron.

	However, earlier signs of problems included a staff protest in June 2024 and an open letter signed by 79 Mucem staffers decrying a toxic workplace, including “rising pressure and threats.”

	The IGAC report states that in addition to one former Mucem worker who filed a formal complaint for sexual and moral harassment by Costa, government auditors discovered a second, allegedly similar case during their investigation.
	

	According to the IGAC, the first unnamed former museum worker said Costa repeatedly made explicit propositions to him on the evening of August 8, 2025. Other employees said they witnessed Costa’s “inappropriate behavior” toward the same worker. The second, former Mucem employee, said they experienced something similar, stating: Costa “made sexual propositions to me, like oral sex, it happened a thousand times … I pushed him away by making jokes about it.”

	Costa has denied all wrongdoing. “I don’t speak to people in that manner,” he told government investigators. In April, he also told Le Monde he had “full confidence” in the ongoing judicial investigation by Marseille’s judicial system. “I want transparency and for everything to be brought to light … These are extremely serious accusations, and I dispute them.”

	Lastly, according to the report, Costa breached fair competition regulations by granting several contracts to individuals and/or companies while also spending well beyond budgeted limits on at least two occasions. These include, but are not limited to, contracts granted at inflated costs to Bastien Baudoin, the head of the consultancy firm Tyrex Conseil, and the company Ludoparc, for the building of a children’s playground. These represent “risks of conflict of interest or criminal offenses,” according to the IGAC report.
	

	In their explanation, the report describes “a president regarded as untouchable as he is incompetent, and an inner circle that is likewise not very competent and failing in its role as a safeguard.”

	Lastly, IGAC investigators recommended launching disciplinary proceedings against Costa and the general manager, Haché.

title: An Obscure Canadian Agency Helped Convict Norval Morrisseau Forgers—and Is Finally Getting Its Due
description: New information has been released by a little-known Canadian federal agency about its staffers’ years-long effort to contribute to a police investig
body:
New information has been released by a little-known Canadian federal agency about its staffers’ years-long effort to contribute to a police investigation into fraudsters selling faked paintings supposedly by Indigenous Canadian artist Norval Morrisseau. 

	CityNews Toronto reports that the largest art fraud case in the history of Canada took at least 1,000 fakes off the market, though there may be thousands more still in private hands. The case made headlines internationally, but the contribution by the Canadian Conservation Institute, an obscure part of the Heritage Department, was previously unreported. The Institute assists some 2,700 museums, libraries, and archival organizations, and, in this case, assisted the Ontario Provincial Police, exposing fakes and ultimately testifying for the prosecution in the trial of one of the fraudsters.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Morrisseau, the unofficial founder of what became known as the Woodland School, died at 75 in 2007. His auction record was set in 2022 when the painting Animal Unity (1978) fetched $312,000 Canadian (about $227,000 at current exchange rates), more than tripling its high estimate, at Canadian auctioneer Cowley Abbott. In his late years, he realized that Toronto art gallery Maslak McLeod and others in Ontario and Alberta were selling fraudulent works under his name. He also disavowed the Morrisseau Family Foundation, formed by his children to authenticate his paintings, but later found to have approved bogus works. 

	The investigation that brought down the fraud rings began when Kevin Hearn, keyboardist for Canadian rock band Barenaked Ladies, bought a supposed Morrisseau from Maslak McLeod in 2005 and lent it to the Art Gallery of Ontario in 2010. Curator Gerald McMaster suspected that it was not genuine, and Hearn’s lawyer, Jonathan Sommer, soon found that the gallery had given a fictitious provenance for the work. The piece was also signed on the back, which was not the artist’s practice. Hearn sued and won a $60,000 judgment but has been unable to collect; the gallery owner died while the case was in court.

	A 2019 documentary, There Are No Fakes, drew the attention of authorities by exposing the fraud ring and revealing that Morrisseau’s own family members enlisted child labor to create the paintings. In the National Post, critic Chris Knight called the story as set out in the film “as riveting as it is complicated.” 
	

	The Ontario Provincial Police investigated for more than two years. As part of the investigation, the Canadian Conservation Institute agreed to inspect four potential fakes, which arrived on its doorstep in 2021. Mylène Choquette, senior scientific documentation technologist at the Institute, viewed one of the paintings with a camera that reveals infrared spectra and, to her shock, found the letters R and LB under areas of red and light blue, revealing that the painting was created on canvases marked out by the makers in a fraudster’s equivalent of a paint-by-numbers scheme. 

	“I needed to just step away from the setup and just come back to see if I see it again,” Choquette told CityNews of the moment she spotted the codes. “Indeed, it was still there.” 

	The conservators found not only the R and LB, but also an area marked “medium green.” Conservators also detected polyvinyl acetate and styrene in a speck of paint, while Morrisseau’s confirmed works were made only with acrylic paint. When the police received the conservators’ findings, reports CityNews, they turned over another 26 contested works, which Choquette and her colleagues studied from 2021 to 2023. 

	Police would charge eight people in three suspected fraud rings with 40 charges, including forgery and defrauding the public of more than $5,000. They called David Voss the architect of the scheme and accused Gary Lamont of recruiting Indigenous artists, including Morrisseau’s nephew Benji and other family members. They alleged that the bad actors had created at least 1,000 fakes. Four suspects pleaded guilty, including mastermind David Voss, and Benji admitted guilt and had his case administered through a First Nations restorative justice program, while charges against two were dropped, CityNews notes.
	

	Representatives of the Institute even testified for the prosecution at the trial of Jeff Cowan, who was found guilty of fraud and dealing in forged documents. 

	The Institute kept its work tightly under wraps until this month, when, convinced that learning the story would benefit all Canadians, it invited members of the press to visit its facility. 

	“Norval Morrisseau is one of the most important artists in Canada and his work is culturally significant to every single one of us,” senior conservation scientist Jennifer Poulin told CityNews. “And when an artist like that is picked out and abused and treated this way, it affects the entire country. And it’s really important that we’re able to try to stop this in any way that we can.”

	A 2024 study by insurance company Chubb found that collectors named fraud and provenance concerns as their chief worry.
